title: Maps from a weakly contractible affine to finite constant objects
statement: Let $X$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme] with its small pro-etale site [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site], and let $U$ be an affine object that is weakly contractible, meaning that for every epimorphism $F\to G$ of sheaves of sets on $X_{\mathrm{proet}}$, the map $F(U)\to G(U)$ is surjective. For every profinite set $S$, write $X[S]$ for the pro-etale object obtained as the inverse limit of finite disjoint unions of copies of $X$ indexed by finite quotients of $S$. The connected-component quotient $\pi_0(|U|)$, with its quotient topology, is profinite, and there is a natural bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_X(U,X[S])\cong C(\pi_0(|U|),S)$, compatible with maps in $S$ and with morphisms between such $U$.

proof.text: Apply the existing Mathlib leaf [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-scheme-spectral] to the affine scheme $U$: its quasi-compactness and quasi-separatedness hypotheses are supplied by the affine instances AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.compactSpace_of_isAffine (Mathlib/AlgebraicGeometry/AffineScheme.lean:561) and AlgebraicGeometry.quasiSeparatedSpace_of_isAffine (Mathlib/AlgebraicGeometry/Morphisms/QuasiSeparated.lean:167). Thus its underlying space $T=|U|$ is spectral. This is a specialization using inferred instances, not a new lemma. Thus [def-weil-spectral-space] gives quasi-compactness, a basis of quasi-compact opens, and quasi-compact intersections. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-quasicompact-components-clopen-intersection]: each component is the intersection of its clopen neighbourhoods. If points $x,y$ lie in different components, some clopen $V$ contains $x$ and not $y$. Every clopen is a union of whole components: otherwise a component meeting both $V$ and its complement would have a separation into two nonempty relatively open sets. For the quotient $q:T\to Q=\pi_0(T)$, therefore $q^{-1}(q(V))=V$, and $q(V)$ and its complement are open by the quotient topology. They separate $q(x)$ and $q(y)$, proving Hausdorffness; a connected subset of $Q$ cannot contain two distinct points because of this same clopen separation, proving total disconnectedness. Finally any open cover of $Q$ pulls back to an open cover of $T$, has a finite subcover by quasi-compactness, and this finite family covers $Q$ because $q$ is surjective. Hence $Q$ is compact Hausdorff totally disconnected, that is, profinite. This uses no Hausdorffness of $T$ and no splitting of covers.

proof.text: For a finite discrete set $I$, [lem-weil-pbc-profinite-test-object-functor] applied to the constant one-object finite-quotient presentation of $I$ gives $X[I]=\coprod_I X$. Apply [lem-galois-coproduct-copies-morphisms-clopen] with its base $U$ replaced by $X$, its source $W$ replaced by our $U$, and structure morphism $U\to X$. Its fibre description gives a bijection between $X$-morphisms to $X[I]$ and maps $h:T\to I$ with all fibres open; these are precisely continuous maps to the finite discrete set. Such an $h$ is constant on every connected component, since distinct values would separate it. It thus factors uniquely as $\bar h q$. For every open $B\subseteq I$, $q^{-1}(\bar h^{-1}(B))=h^{-1}(B)$ is open, so the quotient topology proves $\bar h$ continuous. Conversely continuous $\bar h:Q\to I$ gives continuous $\bar h q$. The two constructions are inverses, proving the finite-case bijection. We require continuity of $h$, not merely constancy on components.

proof.text: Choose a small cofiltered presentation $S=\varprojlim_i S_i$ by finite discrete quotient sets, as in [lem-weil-pbc-profinite-test-object-functor]. Its scheme-limit clause gives $X[S]=\varprojlim_i X[S_i]$. An $X$-map from $U$ to this limit is, by the defining universal property of the scheme limit, exactly a compatible family of $X$-maps $U\to X[S_i]$. Apply step 2 at each stage. Compatibility is preserved because the associated function labels the summand containing the image point, and a transition sends the summand labelled $s$ to that labelled by its image. We obtain precisely compatible continuous functions $Q\to S_i$.

proof.text: A compatible family $h_i:Q\to S_i$ defines the unique function $h:Q\to S$ with coordinates $h_i$, since $S$ is the topological inverse limit. The inverse images of basic opens (finite intersections of inverse images of opens of the $S_i$) are finite intersections of open subsets of $Q$; hence $h$ is continuous. Conversely composing a continuous $h$ with the projections gives a compatible continuous family. Together with step 3 this proves the required bijection. If $S$ is empty use the presentation with its empty finite quotient: step 2 gives no maps when $U$ is nonempty and one map when $U$ is empty. For singleton $S$ both sides have one element.

proof.text: For $a:U^{\prime}\to U$ over $X$, the continuous underlying map takes connected components into connected components, and hence induces $\pi_0(a):Q^{\prime}\to Q$; continuity follows by the quotient topology since $\pi_0(a)q^{\prime}=qa$. At a finite target $I$ the function associated to $fa$ is the function associated to $f$ composed with $\pi_0(a)$, by taking preimages of summands. For a continuous $b:S\to S^{\prime}$, take any finite quotient $r:S^{\prime}\to J$. The continuous finite-valued function $rb$ has finite clopen fibres, so factors through a finite quotient $p:S\to I$, with $rb=cp$. The functoriality and limit cone of [lem-weil-pbc-profinite-test-object-functor] give $X[r]X[b]=X[c]X[p]$ (composition written in ordinary map order). The finite-stage correspondence therefore identifies $X[b]f$ with $bh$. Equality at all finite quotients determines the maps to the limits, so the bijection is covariant in $S$ and contravariant in $U$.
